appraisal_events.evidence: Cette déclaration de principes vertueux fit l'effet d'une douche d'eau froide sur le baron... La mauvaise impression du baron fut d'ailleurs accrue par la façon dont le bénéficiaire le remercia... M. de Charlus était à la fois désespéré et exaspéré par cet effort factice vers la perversité... Rien n'est plus limité que le plaisir et le vice... ne faisant que froisser l'amour-propre de M. de Charlus.
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus's search for genuine depravity among the young men is repeatedly deflated: Maurice's sincere family devotion, a companion's clumsy invented 'perversity,' a failed attempt at slang, and finally Jupien's excuse all leave him disappointed, exasperated, and privately stung, while the narrator explicitly comments on how narrow and repetitive vice actually is.

appraisal_events.evidence: on regrettait beaucoup, dans l'établissement, la mort de quelqu'un dont les gigolos disaient : « Je ne sais pas son nom, il paraît que c'est un baron »... C'était un grand bel homme... il passait des heures chez Jupien à bavarder, à raconter des histoires du monde devant des voyous.
appraisal_events.explanation: The prince de Foix is fondly and specifically remembered as a handsome, engaging presence in Jupien's establishment, esteemed there even though the boys did not know his real name or rank and his double life stayed hidden from his own social world—so local warmth coexists with an ironic note of concealment.

status_effects.explanation: Charlus's hoped-for encounter with real transgression collapses repeatedly into disappointment and wounded pride, leaving him locally frustrated despite his earlier flirtatious enjoyment of the scene.

He is recalled with specific fondness as an attractive, sociable figure in Jupien's demimonde, a modest local elevation qualified by the fact that neither his identity nor his true nature was ever recognized there or in society.

ambiguities: The narrator's irony toward Charlus's disappointment leaves some tension over whether the diminishment lands more on Charlus (his exposed, limited fantasy) or reflects favorably on Maurice (whose sincerity is quietly framed as sympathetic); the annotation follows the narrator's explicit 'cercle vicieux' commentary in treating Charlus as the primary target.

The closing paragraph extends the same concealment/hereditary-vice theme to the unnamed 'jeune prince de Foix' (son), including an unconfirmed report ('c'était possible') that he provoked the advance he was suspected in; since this produces no actual public exposure and the son is not on the reference sheet, it is not represented as a separate status-moving event or character entry.
